name: Abu Bakr II sails into the Atlantic
traveler: Mansa Abu Bakr II of Mali
summary: Mansa Musa told the scholars of Cairo that his predecessor, wanting to know whether the ocean had another shore, sent 200 ships into the Atlantic. One came back, its captain telling of a great river in the sea that carried the others away; the king then sailed himself with 2,000 ships and never returned. Whether any reached land is unknown.

stops.note: The king prepares the fleet.
The ships leave the coast of the empire.
A great current carries the ships west, the returning captain reports.
One ship returns; the king sets out himself and is not seen again.

informs.note: A river in the sea, says the one captain who returned

name: Aelius Gallus into Arabia
summary: Augustus sends 10,000 men to seize the incense kingdoms of southern Arabia. Misled, his ally says, by the Nabataean guide Syllaeus, the army marches for months through waterless country, besieges Marib and turns back, beaten by thirst and disease. Strabo, a friend of Gallus, records what they saw.

stops.note: The army embarks on the Red Sea.
Lands on the Nabataean coast; the winter is lost to scurvy.
Captured after a long march through the desert.
A six-day siege of the Sabaean capital, given up for lack of water.
The retreat north.
Home with a seventh of the army lost, almost all to disease.

name: Agricola in Caledonia
summary: As governor of Britain, Agricola pushes Roman power into Scotland, defeats the Caledonians at Mons Graupius and sends his fleet around the north of Britain, proving it an island and sighting Orkney and perhaps Thule. His son-in-law Tacitus tells the story.

stops.note: Agricola arrives as governor.
The druids' island is taken.
The army reaches the Tay.
The Caledonians under Calgacus are defeated: 'they make a desert and call it peace.'
The fleet sails around the north and subdues the Orkneys.
The fleet completes the circuit: Britain is an island.

name: Ahuitzotl's campaigns to Xoconochco
summary: The eighth Mexica ruler drives the Triple Alliance's armies south along the Pacific slope to Xoconochco, the cacao country on the border of Guatemala, opening the road for the pochteca, the long-distance merchants who bring back quetzal feathers, jade and news from as far as Cuauhtēmallān.

stops.note: Ahuitzotl becomes tlatoani.
Huaxyacac, a garrison in the Zapotec valley.
The isthmus and its Zapotec kingdom.
The cacao country is conquered; the pochteca's road reaches Guatemala.
Tribute of cacao, feathers and jaguar skins flows north.

informs.note: Xoconochco and the road to Cuauhtēmallān

name: Alexander's campaign
traveler: Alexander of Macedon and his army
summary: A Macedonian army crosses into Asia, destroys the Persian empire and marches to the Indus. It brings surveyors (bematists) who pace out the roads, and its reports, together with Nearchus' voyage home along the coast, give the Greek world its first first-hand picture of Persia, Central Asia and India.

stops.note: The army, about 40,000 strong, leaves the Macedonian capital.
First victory over the Persian satraps after crossing into Asia.
Alexander cuts the Gordian knot, by the story.
Defeats Darius III, who flees east.
A seven-month siege of the island city.
Consults the oracle of Ammon in the desert.
Founds the city that will become the Greek world's centre of learning.
Decisive defeat of Darius.
The city opens its gates.
The palaces are looted and burned.
Darius is murdered by his own officers.
Two years of hard fighting in Bactria and Sogdiana.
Sogdian resistance under Spitamenes lasts two years.
'Alexandria the Furthest', on the Jaxartes.
The king of Taxila joins him.
Defeats King Porus and his elephants.
The army refuses to go on toward the Ganges, of which it has heard.
The Indus delta; first sight of the Ocean's tides.
A disastrous march through the desert; thousands die.
Nearchus brings the fleet along the coast from the Indus and finds Alexander inland.
Mass weddings of Macedonians and Persians.
Alexander dies, aged 32, planning a voyage around Arabia.

informs.note: The Ganges and the Gangaridai, by report

name: Almagro to Chile
summary: Pizarro's partner leads 500 Spaniards and thousands of conscripted Andean porters south along the Inca roads in search of another Peru. Many porters die crossing the high Andes and the Atacama; Almagro finds no gold and returns to fight Pizarro for Cuzco.

stops.note: Almagro marches south with the Inca prince Paullu as guide.
Along the Qhapaq Ñan by the lake.
Over the Andes in winter; hundreds of porters freeze to death.
Down into the valleys of Chile.
A party pushes as far south as the Maule River; the land is poor in gold.
Back north along the coast through the desert.
Seizes Cuzco from the Pizarros, which leads to civil war and his execution.

name: Amundsen to the South Pole
summary: Amundsen lets his crew believe they are bound for the Arctic, then turns south. With dogs, skis and four companions he reaches the South Pole five weeks before Robert Falcon Scott, whose party dies on the way back.

stops.note: The Fram leaves; the crew think they are bound for the Arctic.
Amundsen tells the crew the real goal and cables Scott: 'Beg leave to inform you Fram proceeding Antarctic.'
Winter base on the Ross Ice Shelf. On 20 October five men set out with four sledges and 52 dogs.
They climb a glacier to the polar plateau and kill most of the dogs to feed the rest.
They reach the pole and leave a tent, Polheim, with letters for King Haakon and for Scott.
Back at base, 99 days after setting out.
The news is cabled to the world.

informs.note: First people at the South Pole
The news reaches Europe from Hobart

name: Apollo 11
traveler: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins
summary: Eight days, 1.5 million kilometres, and the first people to walk on another world. Collins circles the Moon alone while Armstrong and Aldrin spend about two and a half hours outside on the surface.

stops.note: A Saturn V lifts off at 13:32 UTC.
One and a half orbits, then the third stage fires toward the Moon over the Pacific.
Apollo 11 slips into orbit behind the Moon, out of radio contact.
At 20:17 UTC: 'The Eagle has landed.'
At 02:56 UTC Armstrong steps onto the surface; Aldrin follows.
Eagle lifts off and rejoins Collins in Columbia.
The USS Hornet recovers the crew.

informs.note: The first people on another world

name: Askia Muhammad's pilgrimage
summary: The new ruler of Songhay crosses the Sahara with 1,500 men and 300,000 pieces of gold, endows a hostel for West African pilgrims in Mecca, and is named the Abbasid caliph's deputy for the lands of the Sudan. He comes home with scholars and the title of caliph.

stops.note: The pilgrimage sets out.
Through Aïr, by the central Saharan road.
The oases of the Fezzan.
Meets the scholar al-Suyuti and the Abbasid caliph.
Endows a hostel for pilgrims from the Sudan.
Home as the caliph's deputy for the Sudan.

name: Atiśa: Suvarṇadvīpa and Tibet
summary: A Bengali scholar sails to Suvarṇadvīpa (Sumatra) to study for twelve years with the master Dharmakīrti, returns to teach at Vikramaśīla, and in old age crosses the Himalaya at the invitation of the kings of western Tibet. He never returns; his teaching reshapes Tibetan Buddhism.

stops.note: Atiśa sets out for the island of gold.
Takes ship across the Bay of Bengal.
Twelve years with Dharmakīrti at Srivijaya.
Returns to become the monastery's leading teacher.
Sets out for Tibet at sixty.
Received by the king of Guge in western Tibet.
Teaches in central Tibet.
Dies here, never having gone home.

name: Ban Chao in the Western Regions
summary: With a few dozen men and local allies, Ban Chao restores Han control over the oasis kingdoms of the Tarim basin over thirty years. In 97 he sends his officer Gan Ying west to reach Daqin (Rome); Gan Ying gets to the Persian Gulf, where Parthian sailors tell him the sea crossing takes years, and turns back.

stops.note: Ban Chao is sent west with 36 men.
Ban Chao's men kill the Xiongnu envoys, and the king submits.
Khotan joins the Han.
His base for the next twenty years.
Ban Chao becomes Protector General of the Western Regions.
Gan Ying travels west through Parthia.
Told the sea takes up to three years to cross, he turns back.
Ban Chao returns home at seventy and dies a month later.

informs.note: Tiaozhi on the shore of the great sea

name: Barentsz in the Arctic
traveler: Willem Barentsz and Jacob van Heemskerck
summary: Seeking a north-east passage to China, a Dutch crew discovers Bear Island and Spitsbergen, then rounds the north of Novaya Zemlya and is frozen in. They are the first Europeans known to winter in the high Arctic, in a house built from driftwood; Barentsz dies on the way back in open boats.

stops.note: Two ships sail north.
A polar bear is killed; the island is named for it.
'Pointed mountains': the first known sighting of Svalbard.
The ship is crushed in the ice; they build a hut of driftwood.
In June they set out in two open boats; Barentsz dies within a week.
Twelve survivors reach a Dutch ship.
Home.

name: Batu's western campaign
summary: A Mongol army of perhaps 120,000 conquers the Volga Bulghars, the Cumans and the Rus principalities, sacks Kyiv, and drives into Poland and Hungary, destroying two European armies within days of each other in 1241. News of the Great Khan's death turns them back; the Golden Horde rules the Rus for two centuries.

stops.note: The Volga Bulghar capital is destroyed.
The first Rus city to fall.
The grand prince's capital is burned.
The mother of Rus cities is sacked.
A Polish and German army is destroyed.
King Béla's Hungarian army is destroyed.
The pursuit of Béla reaches the Adriatic.
News of Ögedei's death; Batu withdraws and founds his capital on the Volga.

name: The voyage of the Beagle
summary: A Royal Navy survey ship sent to chart the coasts of South America takes along a 22-year-old naturalist. FitzRoy's charts were used for a century; Darwin's notes on fossils, finches and coral reefs led, more than twenty years later, to On the Origin of Species.

stops.note: Sails on a five-year voyage.
Darwin's first look at the geology of a volcanic island.
The tropical forest; Darwin is horrified by slavery.
Fossils of giant extinct ground sloths.
Three Fuegians brought to England on an earlier voyage are returned home.
Two years charting the coast of Patagonia.
Darwin crosses the Andes and finds sea shells near the summits.
An earthquake raises the coast by metres before his eyes.
Five weeks among tortoises and mockingbirds that differ from island to island.
A stop on the voyage.
Darwin is unimpressed by the colonists.
The colony impresses him; the bush does not.
Darwin works out how coral atolls grow on sinking volcanoes.
Meets the astronomer John Herschel.
Home after almost five years.

name: Bering's first Kamchatka expedition
summary: Peter the Great sends a Danish officer across Siberia to find whether Asia and America are joined. After three years hauling supplies overland, Bering builds a ship on Kamchatka and sails north through the strait that bears his name, but fog hides America and he turns back without proof.

stops.note: Sets out overland across Siberia.
Supplies are dragged across rivers and mountains.
A ship is built to cross to Kamchatka.
The St Gabriel is built.
At 67°18′N with no land in sight, Bering turns back.
Back across the Sea of Okhotsk.
Home overland; the question remains open.

name: Bering's Great Northern Expedition to America
traveler: Vitus Bering, Aleksei Chirikov and Georg Steller
summary: From Kamchatka the St Peter and the St Paul sail east and find Alaska. The naturalist Steller has ten hours ashore on Kayak Island. On the way home the St Peter is wrecked on an island where Bering and half the crew die of scurvy; the survivors build a boat from the wreck and bring home sea-otter furs that start the Russian fur trade.

stops.note: The St Peter and the St Paul sail together, then lose each other in a storm.
Steller lands for ten hours and collects the first Alaskan specimens.
Meetings with Unangan people; scurvy spreads.
Wrecked; Bering dies here in December.
46 survivors return in a boat built from the wreck, with otter skins.

name: Cabeza de Vaca across the continent
traveler: Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, Estevanico, Dorantes and Castillo
summary: Of the 300 men of the Narváez expedition stranded in Florida, four survive eight years as castaways, traders and healers among the peoples of the Gulf coast and the Southwest, and walk to Mexico. Their stories of rich cities to the north send Coronado out to look for them.

stops.note: Narváez lands 300 men and sends the ships away.
Starving, they build rafts of horsehide and sail west along the coast.
The rafts are wrecked; the Karankawa take in the survivors.
After six years as slaves and traders, four men escape inland.
Famous as healers, they are passed from village to village.
Villagers tell of great towns to the north and give them turquoise and emeralds.
They meet Spanish slavers, to the soldiers' astonishment.
Received by the viceroy; their report sets off the search for Cíbola.

informs.note: Rumours of rich towns to the north

name: John Cabot to Newfoundland
summary: A Venetian sailing for Henry VII crosses the North Atlantic in the small Matthew and lands on a coast he takes for north-east Asia, five centuries after the Norse. The cod he reports, so thick 'they could be taken with baskets', draws fishermen for centuries. He vanishes on a second voyage in 1498.

stops.note: The Matthew sails with about 18 men.
The last land before the crossing.
Landfall: Cabot plants the banners of England and Venice.
Seas so full of cod they could be taken with baskets.
Home in 15 days; Henry VII gives him £10.

name: Cabrillo up the coast of California
traveler: Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo and Bartolomé Ferrer
summary: Three small ships from New Spain sail up an unknown coast looking for wealth and a passage to Asia. Cabrillo is the first European to enter San Diego Bay and see the coast of California; he dies of an infected wound on the Channel Islands, and his pilot Ferrer pushes on north to about Oregon.

stops.note: Three ships leave the Pacific port of Navidad.
'A very good enclosed port.' The Kumeyaay meet them.
Chumash towns along the coast, with plank canoes.
Storms drive them past without seeing the bay's shelter.
Cabrillo dies of gangrene after a fall.
Ferrer, now in command, reaches perhaps 42°N before turning back.
Home, with no gold and no passage.

name: Caesar's Gallic War
summary: In eight years of campaigns Caesar conquers Gaul from the Pyrenees to the Rhine, bridges the Rhine twice and crosses twice to Britain. His own Commentaries, written for Rome, give the first detailed account of the lands and peoples of the north.

stops.note: Blocks the Helvetii from migrating west.
Defeats the Helvetii.
War with the Belgae.
Defeats the seafaring Veneti in a battle at sea.
Bridges the river in ten days and raids into Germania.
The first crossing to Britain.
A second, larger invasion; Cassivellaunus submits.
The siege that ends Vercingetorix's revolt.
Gaul is a province; the Commentaries are published.

name: HMS Challenger
traveler: Charles Wyville Thomson, John Murray and the crew of HMS Challenger
summary: The first great oceanographic expedition sails 127,000 km, stopping every 200 miles to sound the depth, dredge the floor and take the temperature of the water. It finds over 4,000 new species, maps the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and sounds a trench near Guam deeper than any then known.

stops.note: A warship with most of its guns removed to make room for laboratories.
First deep soundings.
Soundings across the Atlantic reveal a ridge down its middle.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
Dredging the cold southern waters.
The first steamship to cross the Antarctic Circle.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A sounding of about 8,200 metres: the deepest water then known. The deepest part is later named after the ship.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
Home after 1,000 days; the results take 19 years and 50 volumes to publish.

informs.note: The first profile of the ocean floor

name: The Chola fleet against Srivijaya
summary: The Chola emperor of south India sends a fleet across the Bay of Bengal to break the hold of Srivijaya on the straits. His Tanjore inscription lists the ports it sacked, from Kadaram (Kedah) to Sumatra: the furthest overseas campaign of any Indian state.

stops.note: The fleet leaves the Chola port on the Coromandel coast.
Nakkavaram, the naked islands, on the way east.
Kadaram, Srivijaya's port on the peninsula, is taken.
The Srivijayan capital is sacked and its king captured.
The inscription lists port after port along Sumatra's east coast.
Home to the new capital; the conquests are carved on the temple walls.

name: Columbus, second voyage
summary: Seventeen ships carry 1,200 settlers to colonize Hispaniola. Columbus finds the Lesser Antilles, Puerto Rico and Jamaica on the way, explores the south coast of Cuba (which he makes his men swear is the mainland of Asia), and begins the enslavement of the Taíno.

stops.note: Seventeen ships, horses, cattle, sugar cane and 1,200 men.
Landfall in the Lesser Antilles after three weeks.
Kalinago villages.
Borikén, the island of the Taíno.
The fort is burned and all 39 men are dead.
The first Spanish town in the Americas.
Xaymaca, explored along its north coast.
Columbus has his crews swear that Cuba is a mainland.
Back to Spain to answer complaints against his rule.

name: Columbus, third voyage
summary: Sailing further south, Columbus reaches Trinidad and the Gulf of Paria, where the flood of fresh water from the Orinoco tells him he has found 'a very great continent'. He goes on to Hispaniola, where a royal inquiry sends him home in chains.

stops.note: Six ships; three go straight to Hispaniola.
South to find the equator's lands.
Three hills on the horizon; he names the island for the Trinity.
The Orinoco's fresh water: 'I believe this is a very great continent which until today has been unknown.'
The colony is in revolt.
Arrested by Francisco de Bobadilla and shipped home in chains.

informs.note: Columbus at the Gulf of Paria; Ojeda and Vespucci

name: Columbus, fourth voyage
traveler: Christopher Columbus and his son Fernando
summary: Old and ill, Columbus searches for a strait through to the Indian Ocean along the coast of Central America. He finds gold in Veragua and a Maya trading canoe, but worm-eaten ships strand him on Jamaica for a year.

stops.note: Four old ships.
A great Maya trading canoe laden with cloth, copper and cacao.
'Thanks be to God': clear of a month of storms.
Gold, and tales of another sea nine days' march away.
The first settlement on the mainland is driven out by the Ngäbe.
The ships are beached, rotten; a year marooned.
Home. He dies in 1506, still sure he reached Asia.

name: Columbus, first voyage
summary: Looking for a westward route to Asia, Columbus reaches the Bahamas, Cuba and Hispaniola, islands long home to the Lucayan and Taíno peoples. He thinks he is in the Indies. His printed letter spreads the news across Europe within months.

stops.note: 3 August: three ships, the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña.
The last port before the open ocean.
Landfall on an island its Lucayan people call Guanahani; Columbus names it San Salvador.
He wonders whether this is the Asian mainland and sends envoys inland to find the Great Khan.
Larger islands, gold ornaments and the Taíno chief Guacanagarí.
The Santa María runs aground on Christmas Day; 39 men are left behind in a fort built from her timbers.
Sets out for Spain.
After a great storm, the Portuguese briefly arrest part of the crew.
Another storm drives the Niña into Lisbon; Columbus meets King João II.
Home.
Received by Ferdinand and Isabella. His letter is printed and spreads across Europe.

name: Cook's second voyage
traveler: James Cook, with the Resolution and the Adventure
summary: Sent to find the great southern continent, Cook crosses the Antarctic Circle three times and sails further south than anyone before, proving that any southern land must lie under the ice. Between the summers he charts Tonga, Rapa Nui, the Marquesas, Vanuatu and New Caledonia, keeping time with a copy of Harrison's chronometer.

stops.note: The Resolution and the Adventure sail, with Larcum Kendall's copy of Harrison's chronometer.
Last port before the southern ice.
The first ship known to cross the Antarctic Circle.
Rest and repairs in the fiords after four months without sight of land.
Cook calls them the Friendly Islands.
71°10′S, stopped by pack ice: 'I will not say it was impossible anywhere to get farther to the south.'
The great statues, many already toppled.
First European visit since Mendaña in 1595.
Charts the islands he names the New Hebrides.
A large island no European had seen.
Claims the icy island for Britain: 'savage and horrible'.
Home after three years and 110,000 km; the chronometer has kept time.

name: Cook's third voyage
traveler: James Cook, Charles Clerke and Mai
summary: Cook takes Mai home to Huahine, then sails north to look for a passage from the Pacific to the Atlantic. On the way he reaches Hawaiʻi, charts the coast from Oregon to Alaska and through the Bering Strait until the ice stops him. Back in Hawaiʻi he is killed at Kealakekua Bay; Clerke tries the Arctic again and dies off Kamchatka.

stops.note: The Resolution sails; the Discovery under Clerke follows.
Livestock taken on board for the islands.
Adventure Bay, Van Diemen's Land.
Three months in Tonga.
Mai is brought home and settled with a house, horses and a musket.
The first Europeans known to reach Hawaiʻi.
A month among the Mowachaht; sea-otter furs bought for trinkets.
Following the coast north-west, hoping for a passage.
A wall of ice ends the search at 70°44′N.
Cook is killed in a fight on the shore.
Clerke dies of tuberculosis after a second try at the ice.
Sea-otter furs fetch huge prices in China: the start of a fur trade.
Home after four years and three months.

name: Cook's first voyage, with Tupaia
summary: Sent to Tahiti to watch Venus cross the Sun, the Endeavour takes aboard Tupaia, a Raʻiātean navigator and priest. His chart of the islands around Tahiti puts two ways of knowing the Pacific on one sheet of paper. Cook charts Aotearoa and eastern Australia; Tupaia dies at Batavia.

stops.note: The Endeavour sails for the Pacific.
Wine and onions against scurvy.
The Portuguese viceroy suspects them of smuggling.

stops.place: Bay of Good Success, Tierra del Fuego
stops.note: Banks and Solander collect plants; two men die of cold in a snowstorm.
The transit of Venus is observed on 3 June.
Tupaia, navigator and priest from Raʻiātea, joins the ship and pilots it through the islands.
Tupaia directs them south.
Tupaia can speak with Māori. The first meetings end in killings.
A transit of Mercury is observed; Cook charts the coast as he goes.
Cook sails around both islands, showing they are not part of a southern continent.
The Gweagal people resist the landing. Tupaia cannot understand their language.
The ship strikes the Great Barrier Reef and is beached for seven weeks of repairs.
Cook claims the east coast for Britain.
Repairs, malaria and dysentery. Tupaia dies here in December.
Dozens of the crew have died of fever since Batavia.
A last call on the British island before home.
Home with Tupaia's chart, thousands of specimens and new coastlines.

informs.note: News of Tupaia's meetings with Māori reaches Tahiti on Cook's second voyage

name: Coronado and the search for Cíbola
summary: An army of some 350 Spaniards and over 1,000 Indigenous allies from Mexico goes north to find the Seven Cities of Cíbola. They find the Zuni pueblos, made of adobe, not gold; a detachment is led to the rim of the Grand Canyon by Hopi guides; and the main army crosses the Great Plains to Quivira in Kansas before turning back empty-handed.

stops.note: The army musters.
The last Spanish town.
The first Zuni town is stormed. 'Such were the curses that some hurled at Fray Marcos.'
Hopi guides lead García López de Cárdenas to the rim; his men cannot reach the river.
The army winters in the Rio Grande pueblos and wages war on them.
A captive the Spaniards call 'the Turk' promises gold to the east.
Out on the plains, among herds of bison and the Querecho people.
Grass-house villages of the Wichita, with no gold. The Turk is executed.
The broken expedition returns.

informs.note: The Pueblo towns of Cíbola and Tiguex

name: Cortés and the fall of Tenochtitlan
traveler: Hernán Cortés, Malintzin and their Tlaxcalan allies
summary: A few hundred Spaniards land on the Gulf coast, gain thousands of Indigenous allies who resent Mexica rule, and march on Tenochtitlan. With smallpox spreading ahead of them, they destroy the city after a long siege. Cortés's letters to Charles V put Mexico on Europe's map.

stops.note: Cortés sails against the governor's orders with eleven ships.
Finds Gerónimo de Aguilar, a shipwrecked Spaniard who speaks Maya.
After a battle, Malintzin is given to the Spaniards; speaking Nahuatl and Maya, she becomes the indispensable interpreter.

stops.place: Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz
stops.note: Founds a town to claim authority from the Crown and scuttles his ships.
After fierce fighting, the Tlaxcalans, enemies of the Mexica, become allies.
A massacre of the city's people.
Moctezuma receives them in a city of perhaps 200,000 on its lake.
Driven out on the Noche Triste, the Spaniards retreat to their allies. Smallpox spreads through Mexico.
After a 75-day siege the city falls and is razed; Mexico City is built on its ruins.

informs.note: Cortés's letters to Charles V, printed from 1522

name: Vasco da Gama
summary: Four Portuguese ships sail around Africa and, guided across the Arabian Sea by a pilot from Malindi, reach Calicut. The sea route joins Europe's map to an Indian Ocean world that Arab, Indian and Swahili sailors had long known.

stops.note: Four ships leave Restelo.
Water and meat before the open ocean.
A great arc far out to sea to find the westerlies: about three months without sight of land, the longest such passage Europeans had yet made.
First meetings with the Khoikhoi.
Rounded on 22 November.
Music and dancing with the Khoikhoi, then a quarrel over water.
Named on Christmas Day.
The first Swahili port. The sultan takes the Portuguese for Muslims, then turns hostile.
A hostile reception.
The sultan, Mombasa's rival, provides a pilot who knows the monsoon route.
India. Asked what they want, a crewman answers: 'Christians and spices.'
A three-month crossing against the wind. Scurvy kills many of the crew.
Rounded again, homeward.
Home with pepper and news. Two of the four ships and about a third of the men return.

name: Domínguez and Escalante in the Great Basin
traveler: Francisco Atanasio Domínguez and Silvestre Vélez de Escalante
summary: Two Franciscan friars and eight companions set out from Santa Fe to find a road to the new missions of California. Guided by Ute people, they cross the Colorado Plateau and reach Utah Lake before snow turns them back; their map is the first of the Great Basin.

stops.note: Ten men set out, the same summer the thirteen colonies declare independence.
Through the San Juan Mountains.
Guided by the Ute (Timpanogos), they reach a fertile valley and promise a mission.
Snow; they cast lots and decide to turn back.
A ford of the Colorado River they cut steps down to.
A welcome rest.
Home after five months and 2,800 km.

informs.note: The first map of the Colorado Plateau
Utah Lake and word of the lands beyond

name: The settlement of East Polynesia
summary: After a long pause in West Polynesia, double-hulled canoes sail east into the trade winds and, within a few centuries, find almost every habitable island across a triangle bigger than any continent. It is the last great human expansion into empty land. Dates come from radiocarbon and genetics and carry wide error bars.

stops.note: Canoes set out eastward, into the trade wind, so that a voyage that finds nothing can always run home.
Central East Polynesia is reached. Raʻiātea later becomes the sacred centre of voyaging.
Low atolls, hard to see from a canoe, are found and settled.
High islands to the north-east.
Mangareva, Pitcairn and Henderson become linked by a trade in stone tools.
Polynesians and Native Americans meet. Exactly where is unknown; the genetic signal points to this coast. The kūmara (sweet potato) spreads across Polynesia.
The most remote inhabited island on Earth, 2,000 km from its nearest neighbour.
A voyage of 3,800 km north across the equator, steering by stars that change as you go.
The southern Cook Islands.
A stepping stone in the Kermadecs.
The great southern islands, colder and larger than any yet found. The early site at Wairau Bar is shown here.

name: Elissa founds Carthage
summary: A princess of Tyre flees her brother, King Pygmalion, with a band of nobles. They stop in Cyprus and sail on to Africa, where she buys as much land as an oxhide will cover, cuts it into strips and founds Qart-hadasht, the New City. The story is legend; the date fits the archaeology.

stops.note: Elissa's husband is murdered by her brother; she gathers his treasure and her followers.
In Cyprus the priest of Astarte joins them, with eighty young women.
The oxhide is cut into one long strip around the hill of Byrsa. Qart-hadasht, the New City.

name: Ennin's pilgrimage to Tang China
summary: A Tendai monk sails with the last Japanese embassy to Tang China and stays nine years. His diary, the fullest account of Tang China by any foreigner, records travel passes, Korean merchant communities, the holy mountain of Wutai, and the great persecution of Buddhism in 845 that drives him home.

stops.note: The embassy's ships sail for the Tang.
Wrecked near the coast; the embassy goes to Chang'an without him.
He stays behind among Silla Korean merchants.
Pilgrimage to the mountain of Mañjuśrī.
Five years of study in the capital.
The Huichang persecution: monks are laicized and he is expelled.
Home on a Korean ship.

name: Esarhaddon's conquest of Egypt
summary: The king of Assyria marches from Nineveh to the Mediterranean, crosses Sinai with water carried by the camels of Arab kings, and takes Memphis from the Kushite pharaoh Taharqa. For a few years Assyria rules from the Tigris to the Nile.

stops.note: The Assyrian capital.
West across upper Mesopotamia.
Tyre, allied with Taharqa, is put under siege on the way.
The edge of the desert.
Arab kings bring camels and water for the army's crossing.
Memphis falls; Taharqa flees south to Kush, and his family is taken to Nineveh.

name: Hillary and Tenzing Norgay on Everest
summary: A British expedition led by John Hunt, carried by hundreds of porters and Sherpa climbers, puts two men on the highest point on Earth: Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa, and Edmund Hillary, a beekeeper from New Zealand.

stops.note: The expedition sets out on foot with some 350 porters.
The heart of Sherpa country.
Weeks of acclimatization below the monastery.
A route is forced through the Khumbu Icefall.
Tom Bourdillon and Charles Evans turn back about 100 metres below the summit.
At 11:30 Hillary and Tenzing stand on the summit. The news reaches London on the morning of the coronation, 2 June.

name: Faxian's pilgrimage
summary: A Buddhist monk in his sixties walks to India for the monastic rules, then comes home by sea through Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, and is blown far off course to the Shandong coast. His short record is the first Chinese account of the sea route from India.

stops.note: Sets out with four companions.
Crosses the desert, 'with only the bones of the dead to mark the way'.
A grand Buddhist procession.
Over the Pamirs into Gandhara.
A great centre of Buddhist sculpture.
Three years copying texts in the Gupta capital.
Takes ship for the Lion Kingdom.
Two years in Sri Lanka; seeing a fan from China, he weeps with homesickness.
A storm drives the ship to an island where 'heretics and Brahmins flourish'.
Bound for Guangzhou, the ship is blown north for months and lands on the Shandong coast.
Writes the Record of Buddhist Kingdoms.

name: Frobisher's search for the Northwest Passage
summary: Looking for a northern way to Cathay, Frobisher sails into a deep bay in Baffin Island he takes for a strait between Asia and America. He brings back an Inuk captive and black rock thought to hold gold; two more voyages mine 1,350 tons of worthless ore.

stops.note: Two small barks sail.
North around Scotland.
Sights the tip of Greenland, which he takes for Friesland.
Thinks the bay a strait to Asia; five men are lost ashore among the Inuit.
Second and third voyages dig 'gold' ore here.
The ore proves worthless; it ends as road metal.

name: Fu Hao's campaigns
traveler: Fu Hao, consort of King Wu Ding
summary: Fu Hao, a wife of the Shang king Wu Ding, leads armies of thousands against the Tufang in the north, the Qiang in the west and the Ba in the south, as the oracle bones record. Her tomb at Anyang, found intact in 1976, held 130 bronze weapons.

stops.note: The Shang king divines whether Fu Hao should lead the army.
North into the Shanxi highlands against the Tufang raiders.
Home to the capital.
West up the Wei valley against the Qiang.
South to the Han river against the Ba.
She dies before the king and is buried with her weapons, jades and sixteen companions.

informs.note: The Tufang lands of the north

name: Gagarin, Vostok 1
summary: A 27-year-old Soviet pilot makes one orbit of the Earth in 108 minutes. The line on the map is his ground track: the path traced on the surface beneath him.

stops.note: Lift-off at 09:07 Moscow time. 'Poyekhali!' ('Let's go!')
In orbit, climbing toward the most northerly point of the track.
Crossing the Pacific into the night side of the Earth.

stops.place: Near the tip of South America
stops.note: The southernmost part of the orbit.
The retro-rocket fires to bring the capsule down.
108 minutes after launch Gagarin ejects and comes down by parachute in a field.

name: Gao Xianzhi over the Pamirs
summary: A Korean-born Tang general leads 10,000 men across the Pamirs and the Darkot Pass into Gilgit to cut the Tibetan empire off from its allies, one of the hardest mountain campaigns in history. Four years later his army is defeated by the Abbasids at Talas, and the prisoners taken there include Du Huan.

stops.note: The army leaves the Anxi Protectorate.
West to the mountains.
Takes the Tibetan fort at Lianyun on the Wakhan river.
Over a glacier pass at 4,700 metres.
The pro-Tibetan king is captured.
Defeated by the Abbasids and their Karluk allies.
The remnants retreat.

name: Hanno the Navigator
summary: A Carthaginian fleet sails out past the Pillars of Heracles to found colonies down the Atlantic coast of Africa, then explores further south. The account survives only in a short Greek translation, so how far Hanno got (Senegal, Sierra Leone or Cameroon) is still argued over.

stops.note: Sixty ships carrying colonists set out.
The first colony, beyond the Pillars of Heracles.
A wooded headland, where they build a shrine to Poseidon.
Friendly herders act as interpreters for the voyage south.
An island trading post, as far from the Pillars as Carthage is.
A river full of crocodiles and hippopotamuses: perhaps the Senegal.
At night they see fires and hear pipes and drums from the land.
A great burning mountain: perhaps Mount Kakulima in Guinea, or Mount Cameroon.
They capture three 'hairy people' their guides call gorillai, then turn back for want of supplies.

name: Hasekura's embassy to Spain and Rome
summary: The lord of Sendai sends a samurai in a Japanese-built galleon across the Pacific to seek trade with New Spain. Hasekura crosses Mexico, sails to Spain, is baptised before Philip III and received by Pope Paul V in Rome. He comes home seven years later to find Christianity banned.

stops.note: The San Juan Bautista sails with 180 men.
Across the Pacific in three months.
Received by the viceroy; some of his men are baptised.
On to the Atlantic.
With the treasure fleet.
Up the Guadalquivir; stays at Coria del Río, where Japón is still a surname.
Baptised before King Philip III.
Received by Pope Paul V and made a Roman citizen.
Back to Andalusia; the embassy sails for New Spain from Sanlúcar.
Back across the Atlantic with the fleet.
Retracing the road across New Spain.
Sails for Manila on the galleon; sources differ on whether in 1618 or 1619.
Two years waiting in the Philippines.
Home, to a country that has banned Christianity.

name: Hatshepsut's expedition to Punt
summary: Five ships sail down the Red Sea to Punt, the land of incense, and come home with living myrrh trees, ebony, gold, baboons and the chief of Punt's portrait. The queen has it all carved on the walls of her temple.

stops.note: The queen's treasurer Nehesy leads the expedition.
Along the Nile to the start of the desert road.
Across the Wadi Hammamat to the Red Sea, where ships are assembled from parts carried over the desert.
Houses on stilts, incense trees and a chief with his large wife. Punt was probably on the coast of Eritrea or Sudan.
The ships return laden with thirty-one myrrh trees in baskets.
The trees are planted at Deir el-Bahari and the voyage carved on its walls.

name: Hernández de Córdoba to Yucatán
traveler: Francisco Hernández de Córdoba and Bernal Díaz
summary: Sailing from Cuba to capture slaves, three ships find instead the coast of Yucatán, with stone towns and temples larger than anything in the islands. They are beaten off at Champotón; the news of a rich civilization sends Grijalva and then Cortés.

stops.note: Three ships and 110 men.
A town they call 'Great Cairo' for its size.
Temples and painted walls; they are told to leave.
Attacked by Maya warriors; half the men are killed and Córdoba is mortally wounded.
Driven to Florida looking for water.
Córdoba dies of his wounds; his report spreads through Cuba.

name: Hudson and the Half Moon
summary: Hired by the Dutch East India Company to find a north-east passage, Hudson is turned back by ice off Norway and, against orders, sails west instead. He explores the coast from Maine to Chesapeake Bay and the river that now bears his name, opening the way to New Netherland.

stops.note: The Half Moon sails for the North Cape.
Ice and a near-mutiny end the attempt to go east.
Across the Atlantic to the coast of Maine.
South to the English colony's bay, without entering.
Enters the great river and meets the Lenape.
Upriver until the water grows shallow: no passage.
Detained in England with his news.

informs.note: The Hudson River, with Jamestown's Virginia

name: Hudson's last voyage
summary: In the Discovery, Hudson finds the strait and the vast inland sea of Hudson Bay, sure it leads to the Pacific. After a winter frozen in James Bay, his crew mutinies and sets him adrift in a small boat with his son and seven others; they are never seen again.

stops.note: The Discovery sails with 23 men.
The entrance to the strait.
Through the strait into an open sea.
South along the east coast of the bay.
Frozen in for the winter; starvation and quarrels.
The mutineers set Hudson adrift.
Eight survivors bring the Discovery home.

name: Hulagu and the fall of Baghdad
summary: Möngke's brother leads a Mongol army west to subdue the Ismaili fortresses and the Abbasid caliphate. Baghdad falls in 1258 and the last caliph is killed; the advance is stopped by the Mamluks at ʿAyn Jālūt. The Ilkhanate he founds becomes a meeting place of Persian, Chinese and European learning.

stops.note: Hulagu sets out with siege engineers from China.
Through Transoxiana.
The Ismaili castles surrender.
The city is sacked and the caliph al-Mustaʿsim put to death.
Nasir al-Din al-Tusi's observatory is founded under Mongol patronage.
Syria is overrun.
The Mamluks of Egypt defeat the Mongol rearguard.

informs.note: The Mongol world seen from the Ilkhanate

name: Humboldt and Bonpland in the Americas
traveler: Alexander von Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland
summary: A Prussian naturalist and a French botanist carry 42 instruments through the Spanish Americas, measuring altitude, temperature, magnetism and plants as they go. They show how climate and life change with height, and their thirty-volume account remakes Europe's picture of South America.

stops.note: Sail on the Pizarro with royal permission to go anywhere in Spanish America.
Climb the volcano and record how vegetation changes with height.
First landfall in America.
Experiments with electric eels on the grassy plains.
Confirm that the Casiquiare joins the Orinoco to the Amazon basin.
Studies the cinchona trees that give quinine.
Climbs the volcanoes around the city.
Reach about 5,900 metres, higher than anyone known before them; from it Humboldt draws his famous profile of life by altitude.
Measure the cold current offshore, later named after Humboldt.
By sea to New Spain.
A year in New Spain's archives and mines.
Meets President Jefferson, who wants news of Mexico's borders.
Home with 60,000 specimens; publishing takes thirty years.

name: Ibn Battuta
summary: A young legal scholar from Tangier sets out for Mecca and keeps going for 29 years, across some 120,000 km of the Islamic world and beyond it. Back in Fez he dictates the Rihla. A few of its episodes, such as the visit to the Volga, are doubted by scholars.

stops.note: Leaves home at 21 'to make the pilgrimage'. He will be gone 24 years.
Two envoys of the sultan of Tunis join him on the road.
Falls ill with fever and ties himself to his saddle to keep going.
Joins a pilgrim caravan.
Travels with a caravan for safety against raiders.
The great lighthouse is still partly standing.
'Mother of cities', the largest city he has seen.
The Red Sea crossing is blocked, so he goes north through Syria.
Visits the tomb of the Prophet.
His first hajj.
The shrine of Ali.
Shocked to hear the preacher's grammar mistakes in the Friday sermon.
Much of the city in ruins after feuds between factions.
Meets the city's famous ascetic, Majd al-Din.
Still recovering from the Mongol sack of 1258.
The bazaar of the jewellers.
Stays to study.
Takes ship south.
Hot, waterless and rich.
Describes the sultan's court and its enormous meals.
An island town where bananas, lemons and fish are the staple food.
'One of the most beautiful and best-built towns', its houses of wood.
Frankincense and horses for India.
The new island city, rich from the Indian trade.
His third hajj.
Anatolia's Turkish principalities welcome him at every town.
Takes ship across the Black Sea.
A Genoese port; he is alarmed by its church bells.
The moving camp and capital of Özbeg Khan of the Golden Horde.
Escorts the Khan's Byzantine wife, Princess Bayalun, on a visit home.
Its mosques and colleges still damaged from the Mongols.
'One of the greatest and finest cities', though many palaces lie in ruin.
Still in ruins after Genghis Khan.
Crosses the Hindu Kush, which he says means 'slayer of Indians'.
Reaches the Indus.
Serves as a judge under Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq for eight years.
Sent as envoy to China; the junks are wrecked in a storm before he boards.
Becomes a judge, marries into the ruling family and leaves after a quarrel.
Climbs to the footprint at the summit.
Cheap rice and fruit; he calls it 'a hell full of good things'.
A Muslim sultan gives him a junk for China.
'One of the greatest ports in the world, or rather the greatest.'
A city so big it takes three days to cross.
Leaves China.
Back on the long sea road west.
Last sight of India.
Frankincense and horses for India.
Passes through on the way west.
The Black Death kills thousands a day.
His last hajj.
Back in the city where his travels first impressed him.
The last stage before home.
Home. His mother has died of the plague a few months before.
Visits al-Andalus.
Sets out across the Sahara.
A town whose houses and mosque are built of salt slabs.
He is offended by the governor's manners, and surprised that women here go unveiled.
Eight months at the court of Mansa Sulayman, Musa's brother. The city's site is still uncertain.
Sees the tomb of the poet es-Saheli.
'One of the finest towns in the land of the Sudan.'
A copper-mining town.
Called home by the sultan, who sets the scholar Ibn Juzayy to write down his story.

name: Ibn Fadlan's embassy to the Volga
summary: Secretary of an Abbasid embassy to the king of the Volga Bulghars, Ibn Fadlan crosses the frozen steppe of the Oghuz Turks and writes the most vivid early description of the Rus, including a ship burial.

stops.note: The embassy leaves the caliph's court.
Through the Zagros by the old Khorasan road.
Rayy, near today's Tehran.
The great city of Khorasan.
Received by the Samanid emir.
Winter so cold that beards freeze to blocks of ice.
Among the Oghuz Turks, whose customs he describes with curiosity and disapproval.
Crossing the rivers on rafts of camel skin.
Meets the Volga Bulghar king, and the Rus traders, whose chieftain's ship burial he witnesses.
Returns; his report (the Risala) is written down.

informs.note: The homeland of the Rus, by report

name: Inō Tadataka surveys Japan
summary: A retired sake brewer who took up astronomy at fifty spends seventeen years walking Japan's coasts with his survey team, measuring distances with ropes and wheels and fixing latitude by the stars. His maps, finished after his death in 1821, are accurate to within a fraction of a degree.

stops.note: The first survey sets out for Ezo.
The south coast of Ezo.
The coasts of Mutsu and Dewa.
The western coasts.
Kyushu and its islands.
The last survey ends; the great map is completed in 1821.

informs.note: Inō's map of the whole country

name: Daikokuya Kōdayū across Russia
summary: A merchant captain's ship drifts for eight months to the Aleutians. Kōdayū and his surviving crew spend ten years crossing Siberia to St Petersburg, where Catherine the Great receives him and lets him go home. Questioned in Edo, his account becomes Japan's first detailed knowledge of Russia.

stops.note: The Shinshō-maru sails for Edo with rice.
Wrecked in the Aleutians after drifting for eight months.
Taken to Kamchatka; many of the crew die of scurvy.
Across the Sea of Okhotsk.
Meets the naturalist Erik Laxman.
Received by Catherine the Great at Tsarskoye Selo.
Back across Siberia.
Brought home by Adam Laxman's embassy.

name: Kolaios is blown to Tartessos
summary: A Samian merchant bound for Egypt is driven west by an east wind, all the way through the Pillars of Heracles to Tartessos, a market no Greek had traded with. He came home with the richest cargo any Greek had ever carried, and dedicated a tenth of it at the temple of Hera.

stops.note: Bound for Egypt.
An island off Libya, where he leaves supplies for colonists from Thera.
An east wind that will not stop carries him through the Pillars to Tartessos, rich in silver.
Home with sixty talents; a bronze cauldron with griffin heads is made for Hera's temple.

name: The Yuan fleet to Java
traveler: Shi Bi, Ike Mese and Gao Xing
summary: Kublai Khan sends a fleet of perhaps 1,000 ships and 20,000 men to punish the king of Singhasari, who had branded the Khan's envoy. They arrive to find him dead, are drawn into a local war, and are driven out by Raden Wijaya, who goes on to found Majapahit.

stops.note: The fleet sails from Zaitun.
Along the coast of Champa.
The fleet gathers off Belitung.
The army lands on Java's north coast.
Allied with Raden Wijaya, they defeat the king of Kediri.
Wijaya turns on them; they fight their way back to the ships.
Home with a third of the army lost.

name: La Condamine down the Amazon
summary: After eight years measuring a degree of latitude near Quito to settle the shape of the Earth, La Condamine goes home the long way: down the Amazon on a raft and canoes, mapping the river with compass and astronomy. He brings rubber and curare to the notice of European science.

stops.note: The French geodesic mission has measured an arc of the meridian.
Shoots the gorge of the Marañón on a raft.
Fixes positions by the stars as he goes.
Hears of a channel linking the Amazon to the Orinoco.
Measures the tides at the mouth.
On to French Guiana and home to Paris in 1745.

informs.note: La Condamine's map of the river

name: Leif Erikson to Vinland
summary: Norse Greenlanders sail west and winter in a land of grapes and timber. The knowledge stays in the sagas of the far north, reaches the rest of Europe as a rumour in Adam of Bremen, and fades. Five centuries later the Americas have to be found again.

stops.note: Leif buys the ship of Bjarni Herjólfsson, who had sighted land to the west, and sets out with 35 men.
'Land of flat stones': probably Baffin Island.
'Land of forests': probably Labrador.
They winter where there are grapes and timber. The Norse site at L'Anse aux Meadows, found in 1960, fits the sagas.
Home with timber and grapes. Later voyages try to settle, then give up.

informs.note: Known in Greenland and Iceland; reaches the rest of Europe through Adam of Bremen, c. 1075

name: Lewis and Clark's Corps of Discovery
traveler: Meriwether Lewis, William Clark, Sacagawea and York
summary: A U.S. Army company sent by Jefferson to find a water route to the Pacific and to map the lands bought from France. Guided and helped by many Native nations, among them the Shoshone woman Sacagawea, they reach the Pacific and come back with maps, specimens and the news that no easy route exists.

stops.note: About 45 men start up the Missouri.
First council with Oto and Missouria leaders.
Winter among the Mandan and Hidatsa; Sacagawea and Toussaint Charbonneau join.
A month to haul the boats around the falls.
They cross the Continental Divide; the Shoshone chief turns out to be Sacagawea's brother.
Near starvation crossing the Bitterroot Mountains in snow.
The Nez Perce feed them and keep their horses.
'Ocian in view! O! the joy.' Winter on the Pacific coast.
Back after 28 months, long given up for dead.

name: Li Guangli's war against Dayuan
summary: To get the 'heavenly horses' of Ferghana, Emperor Wu sends an army 4,000 km west. The first campaign fails in the desert; the second, with 60,000 men, besieges the capital of Dayuan until its nobles kill their king and hand over the horses. Han power reaches the edge of Central Asia.

stops.note: Emperor Wu names Li Guangli 'Ershi general' after the city of Ershi, where the horses are kept.
The gateway to the west.
The first army, starved by the oasis states, turns back.
A second army of 60,000 sets out.
After a 40-day siege the nobles kill their king and hand over 3,000 horses.
The 'heavenly horses' reach the capital.

informs.note: The war of the Heavenly Horses against Dayuan

name: Livingstone crosses Africa
traveler: David Livingstone and his Makololo companions
summary: A Scottish missionary-doctor, with men lent by the Makololo chief Sekeletu, walks from the upper Zambezi to the Atlantic, then back across the whole continent to the Indian Ocean. Along the way he is shown Mosi-oa-Tunya, which he names Victoria Falls.

stops.note: Sekeletu provides 27 men for the journey west.
Fever almost every week.
Reaches the Atlantic, exhausted, and turns back to bring his companions home.
Back with his companions, as promised, a year later.
'The smoke that thunders.' He names it after his queen.
A Portuguese outpost on the lower Zambezi.
The Indian Ocean: the first recorded crossing of southern Africa by a European.

name: Magellan–Elcano
traveler: Ferdinand Magellan and Juan Sebastián Elcano
summary: Five ships set out to reach the Spice Islands by sailing west. Magellan finds the strait at the tip of South America and dies in the Philippines; Elcano brings one ship and eighteen men home. The voyage reveals how vast the Pacific is.

stops.note: Five ships and about 270 men.
Last supplies in the Canaries.
Rest and fresh food from the Tupi people.
They search the estuary for a passage west and find only fresh water.
Winter. A mutiny is crushed; one ship is wrecked scouting the coast.
The entrance to the strait.
Three ships come out into an ocean Magellan names the Pacific. A fourth has deserted.
An uninhabited atoll. For months the crew have eaten biscuit dust, rats and leather; many die of scurvy.
Food and water from the Chamorro people, then a violent clash.
The Philippines.
Rajah Humabon and hundreds of his people are baptized.
Magellan is killed fighting the warriors of Lapulapu.
A great court with elephants.
The Spice Islands at last. They load cloves.
The Victoria sails on alone under Elcano; the Trinidad stays behind and is lost.
Elcano keeps far south to avoid Portuguese ships.
Rounded after weeks of storms.
Thirteen men sent ashore for food are seized by the Portuguese.
The Victoria returns with 18 men, the first ship to sail around the world.

name: Mamiya Rinzō to Sakhalin and the Amur
summary: Sent by the shogunate to find whether Karafuto (Sakhalin) is an island, Mamiya travels north with Ainu and Nivkh guides, finds the narrow strait that separates it from the mainland, and crosses to the Amur to visit the Qing trading post at Deren.

stops.note: Crosses from the northern tip of Ezo.
South Sakhalin, among the Ainu.
Reaches the narrows: Karafuto is an island.
The Qing trading post where Nivkh and Ainu bring furs.
Home; his maps name the strait that Europeans later call Tatar.

name: Mansa Musa's hajj
summary: The king of Mali crosses the Sahara to Mecca with a caravan of thousands and so much gold that its price in Cairo stays low for years. Cairo's chroniclers write Mali into the Islamic world's geography, and within fifteen years a crowned African king appears on Mediterranean charts.

stops.note: The caravan leaves the capital of Mali. Niani is one candidate for its site; the capital has not been located for certain.
The last town before the desert.
Oases of the central Sahara.
He gives away and spends so much gold that its value in Cairo falls for years, al-Umari reports.
Performs the hajj.
Out of money, he borrows from Cairo's merchants at high interest for the journey home.
Mali's general has taken Songhay's capital; Musa visits.
Commissions the Djinguereber mosque, said to be designed by the Andalusian poet Abu Ishaq es-Saheli.
Home.

informs.note: Cairo, as Mali's court came to know it
'Rex Melly' appears on Dulcert's chart; the Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows Musa holding a gold nugget

name: Nain Singh's secret survey to Lhasa
summary: Trained by the Survey of India and disguised as a Ladakhi trader, a schoolmaster from Kumaon walks to Lhasa counting every step on a 100-bead rosary and hiding his compass in a prayer wheel. He fixes the latitude and height of Lhasa and maps the Tsangpo for 800 km.

stops.note: Trained at the Survey's headquarters: 2,000 paces to the mile.
Sets out as a trader.
Joins a caravan along the Tsangpo.
The Panchen Lama's seat.
Three months in Lhasa; fixes its latitude by the stars from his lodgings.
West along the Tsangpo to its source.
Home with 1,200 miles of route survey.

name: Napoleon's expedition to Egypt
traveler: Bonaparte's army and the Commission of Sciences and Arts
summary: A French invasion of Ottoman Egypt that ends in military failure but brings along 167 scholars, engineers and artists. They measure, draw and collect everything, find the Rosetta Stone, and publish the Description de l'Égypte: the first systematic survey of a whole country outside Europe.

stops.note: Some 35,000 soldiers and 167 savants sail in secret.
Taken from the Knights of St John on the way.
The army lands and storms the city.
After the Battle of the Pyramids, the Institut d'Égypte is founded in the city.
Nelson destroys the French fleet; the army is stranded.
Desaix's column, with the artist Vivant Denon, reaches the temples of Upper Egypt.
The southern limit of the survey.
Soldiers find a stone inscribed in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek; it will unlock the hieroglyphs in 1822.
The Syrian campaign stalls at Acre; Bonaparte slips back to France in August.
The French surrender to the British; the Rosetta Stone goes to London, the notes to Paris.

name: Necho's Phoenicians sail round Africa
traveler: Phoenician sailors, for Pharaoh Necho II
summary: Pharaoh Necho sends Phoenician ships south from the Red Sea with orders to come home by the Pillars of Heracles. Each autumn they land, sow and wait for the harvest; in the third year they reach Egypt again. Herodotus did not believe their report that the noon sun stood on their right, which is the best evidence they told the truth.

stops.note: Necho, who has also begun a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, sends them south.
Down the coast of eastern Africa.
They land, sow grain and wait for the harvest before sailing on.
Sailing west round the continent, they see the noon sun to the north, on their right hand.
Another landing, another harvest, on the Guinea coast.
Into the Mediterranean in the third year.
Home to Egypt. Their story reaches Herodotus a century and a half later.

name: Nero's centurions up the Nile
traveler: Two praetorian centurions sent by Nero
summary: Nero sends a small party up the Nile to look for its source. Helped by the king of Meroë, they pass far beyond Egypt and reach immense marshes, the Sudd, where the river is choked with vegetation that no boat can pass.

stops.note: The party sets out up the Nile.
The edge of Roman Egypt.
The Kushite king provides guides and letters to the rulers beyond.
Endless marshes where 'the plants are so entangled that the water cannot be crossed on foot or by boat.'
They report to Nero.

name: Oñate settles New Mexico
summary: Oñate leads some 500 settlers, soldiers and friars with 7,000 head of livestock up the Camino Real to found the colony of New Mexico. He destroys Acoma Pueblo after a revolt and sends parties east to the plains and west to the Gulf of California.

stops.note: The colonists gather on the northern frontier.
Crosses the Rio Grande and claims New Mexico for Spain.
The first Spanish capital, in a Tewa pueblo.
After Acoma resists, Oñate's men storm the mesa; hundreds are killed or enslaved.
An expedition east to the Wichita villages Coronado saw.

name: Orellana down the Amazon
traveler: Francisco de Orellana and Gaspar de Carvajal
summary: Sent downriver for food from Gonzalo Pizarro's starving expedition east of Quito, Orellana and about 50 men cannot get back against the current and keep going, the first Europeans to travel the Amazon from the Andes to the sea. Carvajal's account of populous river towns and warrior women gives the river its name.

stops.note: Gonzalo Pizarro's expedition sets out to find the Land of Cinnamon.
Orellana takes a brigantine downstream to find food.
No way back against the current.
Long, crowded river towns of the Omagua.
Black water meets white.
Fighting warriors led, Carvajal says, by women.
The open sea, 3,500 km later.
Along the coast to the Spanish pearl island.

name: Monsoon trade (the Periplus route)
summary: An anonymous merchant's handbook describes the ports from the Red Sea to India and down the African coast, and how ships cross open water on the seasonal winds. It is a route rather than a single voyage, so its stops are composite.

stops.note: Goods leave the capital of Roman Egypt up the Nile.
From the Nile, caravans cross the desert to the Red Sea ports.
Ships bound for India leave in July to catch the monsoon.
The port of Aksum: ivory and tortoiseshell.
An Arab market town near the straits.
Once the meeting point of Indian and Egyptian ships.
The Cape of Spices at the tip of the Horn.
Cinnamon, tortoiseshell and slaves on the Somali coast.
The last market town of Azania. Beyond it, the author says, the ocean is unexplored and curves round to the west.
Settled by Arab, Indian and Greek traders.
The frankincense harbour of Dhofar.
Port at the mouth of the Indus.
The busiest port of western India, with pilots to guide ships through its tides.
Pepper port of the Chera kingdom. Some ships sail here directly from Arabia on the monsoon.
The southern tip of India.
A market town on the east coast; Roman pottery has been dug up at nearby Arikamedu.
Known only by report, like Chryse beyond it and, far inland, Thinae, where silk is made.
Ships return on the north-east monsoon from November.

name: Pizarro and the fall of the Inca
summary: With 168 men, Pizarro lands in an Inca empire torn by civil war and smallpox. At Cajamarca he seizes the emperor Atahualpa, takes a room full of gold as ransom, executes him anyway and marches on to Cuzco. The news, and the gold, reach Seville in 1534.

stops.note: Three ships and about 180 men sail south.
The Inca town they saw in 1528 is in ruins from the civil war.
The first Spanish town in Peru.
Atahualpa is ambushed and seized in the square; thousands of his attendants are killed.
Hernando Pizarro loots the great oracle shrine.
Atahualpa, his ransom paid, is garrotted.
Along the Inca royal road, the Qhapaq Ñan.
The Inca capital is entered and stripped of its gold.

name: Marco Polo
summary: A Venetian merchant's son goes east at seventeen and comes home at forty-one. In a Genoese prison he dictates a book about Kublai Khan's empire, and that book carries Cathay, Quinsay and Cipangu onto European maps.

stops.note: Marco, aged 17, leaves with his father Niccolò and uncle Maffeo, who have been to China once already.
They collect holy oil from Jerusalem, as Kublai Khan had asked.
The port of Lesser Armenia.
Through Greater Armenia, past a mountain where Noah's ark is said to rest.
A great market of the Ilkhanate.
Turquoise mines and fine embroidery.
They find the ships sewn with coconut twine and too flimsy to trust, and turn back to go overland.
'A noble city', still in ruins from the Mongol conquest.
Marco falls ill and recovers in the mountain air over a year.
A high plain where fire burns poorly and wild sheep carry huge horns.
Gardens, vineyards and cotton.
Jade from its rivers.
A month to cross the desert, where voices are said to lure travellers off the road.
A Buddhist oasis at the desert's edge.
They stay a year on unexplained business.
Kublai's summer capital, with a cane palace held up by silk cords.
Marco enters the Khan's service and learns several languages.
Missions to the far south-west, towards Burma.
He claims to have governed the city for three years; Chinese sources do not mention him.
'The finest and noblest city in the world', with twelve thousand bridges.
Sails with fourteen ships escorting the princess Kököchin to her bridegroom in Persia.
A kingdom that pays tribute to the Khan in elephants.
Five months waiting for the monsoon; he calls Sumatra 'Java the Less'.
Rubies, and the mountain with Adam's footprint.
Pearl divers of the Gulf of Mannar.
Pepper and brazilwood.
Of the six hundred who sailed, a few dozen survive.
News arrives that Kublai Khan has died.
Robbed of part of their goods.
Through the Bosporus toward home.
Home after 24 years; their relatives do not recognize them.
Captured in a sea battle, he dictates his book in prison to Rustichello of Pisa.

informs.note: Cipangu, an island of gold, by report

name: Ponce de León to Florida
traveler: Juan Ponce de León and Antón de Alaminos
summary: The governor of Puerto Rico sails north-west to find the rumoured island of Bimini. He lands on a coast he names La Florida, and his pilot Alaminos discovers the Gulf Stream, which later carries the treasure fleets home.

stops.note: Three ships sail.
Through the islands, depopulated by slave raids.
Lands at Easter (Pascua Florida) and names the land.
A current so strong it drives the ships backwards: the Gulf Stream.
Round the keys to the west coast; fights with the Calusa.
Home. In 1521 he returns to settle and is killed by a Calusa arrow.

name: Powell down the Colorado
traveler: John Wesley Powell and nine men
summary: A one-armed Civil War veteran leads four boats down the Green and Colorado rivers through the last blank on the map of the United States, the canyons of the Colorado Plateau. Three men who leave the river near the end are killed; the rest emerge after 99 days.

stops.note: Four wooden boats and ten men launch.
The No Name is smashed; a third of the food is lost.

stops.place: Confluence of the Green and Grand
stops.note: Where the Green meets the Grand to form the Colorado.
Calm water between sculpted walls.
'We are now ready to start on our way down the Great Unknown.'
Three men climb out rather than run the rapid; they are killed on the plateau.
The six who stayed on the river reach the settlements.

informs.note: The last blank: the Colorado canyons

name: Pytheas of Massalia
summary: A Greek astronomer sails out past the Pillars of Heracles, circles Britain and hears of Thule, an island six days north where the sea turns thick. His book is lost and later writers called him a liar, but the north never quite left the map again.

stops.note: Sets out from the Greek colony at the mouth of the Rhône.
Past the Pillars of Heracles and into the Ocean, a route Carthage tried to keep closed.
The far western tip of Gaul.
Visits the tin traders and describes how they carry tin to a tidal island to sell.
The northern headland of Britain.
Six days north lies Thule, where the summer night barely falls and the sea becomes a thick 'sea-lung'. Iceland, Norway and Shetland have all been proposed.
The southeastern corner of Britain; he estimates the island's whole circuit, roughly correctly.
An island he calls Abalus, where amber washes up in spring: perhaps Heligoland or the Jutland shore.
Home, perhaps overland by the rivers of Gaul. He writes On the Ocean, which survives only in the quotations of sceptics.

name: The Qing conquest of Dzungaria
traveler: Zhaohui and the Qianlong emperor's armies
summary: The Qianlong emperor sends armies into Dzungaria and the Tarim basin, destroying the last steppe empire; most of the Dzungar people die in the war and the epidemics that follow. The new territory is called Xinjiang, 'new frontier', and surveyed by Jesuit and Chinese mapmakers.

stops.note: The Qing armies assemble in the north-west.
The Dzungar capital falls without a fight.
The rebel Amursana flees to Russia; the Dzungars are destroyed.
The Tarim oases, under the Khoja brothers, resist.
Zhaohui is besieged at the 'Black Water camp' before relief arrives.
Kashgar is taken; the Khojas flee to Badakhshan.

name: Roosevelt and Rondon on the River of Doubt
summary: The Brazilian engineer Rondon, who had strung telegraph lines across Mato Grosso, and the former U.S. president descend an unmapped river of a thousand kilometres. Rapids wreck the canoes, one man drowns, another is murdered, and Roosevelt nearly dies of fever; the river is renamed the Rio Roosevelt.

stops.note: The expedition sets out north across the plateau.
Seven canoes launch on the River of Doubt.
Weeks of portages; a canoe and the paddler Simplício are lost.
Roosevelt, feverish, is carried on.
Down the Madeira to the Amazon.

informs.note: The River of Doubt is mapped

name: Jebe and Subutai's great raid
traveler: Jebe and Subutai, generals of Genghis Khan
summary: Sent after the fleeing Khwarazm-shah, two Mongol generals with about 20,000 horsemen ride around the Caspian Sea, through Persia and the Caucasus onto the steppe north of the Black Sea, crush the Rus princes at the Kalka and return east: a reconnaissance in force of some 8,000 km.

stops.note: Genghis Khan sends Jebe and Subutai after Shah Muhammad.
Through Khorasan.
The city is sacked.
Bought off with tribute.
Through the Caspian Gates into the steppe.
The Rus princes and Cumans are routed.
Turned back by the Volga Bulghars.
They rejoin Genghis Khan with knowledge of the West.

name: Teixeira up the Amazon
traveler: Pedro Teixeira and Cristóbal de Acuña
summary: A Portuguese fleet of 47 canoes with 70 soldiers and 1,200 Indigenous paddlers and archers goes up the Amazon to Quito, the first expedition to travel the river upstream, then comes back down with the Jesuit Acuña, whose book describes the river and its peoples.

stops.note: 47 canoes set out.
Upstream against the current.
Up the Napo toward the Andes.
The Spaniards in Quito are astonished.
Teixeira marks a boundary for Portugal on the way down.
Home after two years; Acuña's book appears in 1641.

informs.note: Acuña's New Discovery of the Great River

name: Trajan to the Persian Gulf
summary: Trajan takes Armenia and Mesopotamia from Parthia, captures its capital Ctesiphon and sails down the Tigris to the Persian Gulf. Seeing a ship leave for India, he is said to have wished he were young enough to follow Alexander. Revolts force him back and he dies on the way home.

stops.note: The army gathers in Syria.
Armenia is annexed.
Northern Mesopotamia is taken.
The Parthian capital falls.
At the head of the Gulf he watches a ship sail for India.
Turning back to crush revolts, Trajan dies.

name: Trieste to the Challenger Deep
summary: Two men sealed inside a steel sphere slung beneath a float of gasoline sink nearly eleven kilometres to the floor of the Mariana Trench, the deepest point of the ocean. No one returns there for 52 years.

stops.note: The bathyscaphe Trieste is towed out by the USS Wandank.
At 08:23 Piccard and Walsh begin to descend.
At 13:06 they touch bottom at about 10,900 metres. An outer window has cracked on the way down. They report seeing a flatfish.
Back on the surface at 16:56, after nine hours.

informs.note: The deepest point of the ocean

name: Tupac Yupanqui: north to Quito and out to sea
summary: Pachacuti's son leads the Inca armies north through the Chimú kingdom to Quito. On the coast, the chroniclers say, he heard of islands to the west, built a fleet of balsa rafts and sailed for nearly a year, returning with dark-skinned captives, gold and a horse-like skin. The islands may have been the Galápagos; the story may be legend.

stops.note: The campaigns north begin.
The Chimú kingdom is conquered.
The northern frontier of Tawantinsuyu.
Raft fleets at the Pacific coast.
Islands to the west, perhaps the Galápagos.
Home after almost a year at sea, the chroniclers say.

name: Vancouver surveys the Northwest Coast
summary: A former midshipman of Cook's spends three summers charting every inlet of the coast from California to Alaska, proving there is no passage to the Atlantic in these latitudes. His survey of Puget Sound and the island that bears his name is the basis of every later chart.

stops.note: The Discovery and the Chatham sail.
Charts part of Australia's south-west coast on the way.
The first of three winters in the islands.
Charts the sound and names it for his lieutenant, Peter Puget.
Negotiates with Bodega y Quadra over Spain's and Britain's claims.
Misses Alexander Mackenzie, arriving overland, by a few weeks.
Proves that Cook's 'river' is a closed inlet.
The last long inlet; no passage anywhere.
Home by Cape Horn.
Home after four and a half years.

name: Vizcaíno charts the California coast
traveler: Sebastián Vizcaíno and Antonio de la Ascensión
summary: Sixty years after Cabrillo, Vizcaíno is sent to find harbours for the Manila galleons on their way home. His charts and the names he gives (San Diego, Monterey, Santa Barbara) stay on Spanish maps for a century and a half.

stops.note: Three ships sail north.
Renames Cabrillo's San Miguel after San Diego.
Names the channel for Saint Barbara.
Praises the bay, too generously, as a fine harbour for the galleons.
Scurvy cripples the crews; one ship reaches about 43°N.
Home with charts that later Spaniards rely on.

name: Wenamun's voyage to Byblos
summary: A priest of Amun is sent to buy cedar for the god's sacred boat. He is robbed at Dor, kept waiting for months at Byblos, where the prince reminds him that Egypt no longer commands, and blown to Cyprus, where the papyrus breaks off.

stops.note: Sent by the high priest Herihor to fetch cedar for Amun's barque.
Smendes, ruler of the north, puts him on a Syrian ship.
A sailor runs off with his silver; the prince of the Tjeker will not help.
He seizes silver from a Tjeker ship in return.
Prince Zakar-Baal makes him wait a month a day and asks for payment first: Egypt's word is no longer enough.
Driven by the wind to Cyprus, where the queen Hatiba saves him from a mob. The story ends here.

informs.note: The Phoenician ports, where Egypt is no longer obeyed

name: Xuanzang's pilgrimage to India
summary: A young monk slips out of Tang China without permission to find better Buddhist texts. Sixteen years later he returns with 657 of them and dictates a record of 138 countries that maps India for China in detail.

stops.note: Leaves secretly; travel abroad has been forbidden.
Slips past the frontier guards at night.
Crosses the Gobi alone on an old red horse and nearly dies of thirst.
The first oasis beyond the desert.
The king of Gaochang begs him to stay and teach; he goes on hunger strike to be let go.
A Buddhist kingdom famous for its musicians.
Crosses the Tian Shan; many of his party die in the snow.
Received by the khagan of the Western Turks in his felt tent.
An oasis city on the road west.
A great trading city, not yet Buddhist.
The Nava Vihara monastery.
Sees the great standing Buddhas, then gilded.
Once a Buddhist heartland, now with many ruined monasteries.
Two years of study.
A centre of Buddhist sculpture.
Capital of King Harsha.
Birthplace of the Buddha, already in ruins.
The deer park at Sarnath where the Buddha first taught.
The tree of the enlightenment.
Studies under the abbot Silabhadra for five years.
A port where he hears of Sri Lanka but does not go.
The far south of his travels.
Harsha holds a great assembly in his honour.
Crosses the Pamirs; loses his elephant and many texts at a river crossing.
The western gate of the Tarim basin.
Writes to the emperor to ask pardon for having left.
Waits here for the emperor's reply.
Returns with 657 texts. Emperor Taizong asks him to write down everything he saw.

informs.note: The Great Tang Records on the Western Regions

name: Yermak's campaign across the Urals
summary: A band of Cossacks hired by the Stroganov merchants crosses the Urals and takes Qashliq, capital of the Khanate of Sibir. Yermak dies in an ambush, but Russia's advance across Siberia to the Pacific follows within sixty years.

stops.note: About 540 Cossacks set out by river boat.
They drag their boats over the watershed.
Down the Tura and Tobol into Sibir.
Firearms decide the battle against Khan Kuchum's army.
The capital of Sibir is taken.
Envoys bring Ivan IV furs and news of the conquest.
Yermak drowns during a night attack, weighed down, the story says, by his armour.

name: Zhang Qian's mission to the west
summary: Sent to find allies against the Xiongnu, Zhang Qian is captured twice and gone for thirteen years. He brings back no alliance, but his report opens Central Asia to Han China and starts the trade later called the Silk Road.

stops.note: Emperor Wu sends him west with about a hundred men to find the Yuezhi.
He leaves Han territory.
Captured by the Xiongnu and held for about ten years. He marries and has a son, but keeps the envoy's staff.
Escapes west. Dayuan has walled cities, grape wine and the 'blood-sweating' horses.
The people of Kangju guide him on to the Yuezhi.
The Yuezhi are settled and prosperous north of the Oxus and have no wish for revenge.
In the markets he sees bamboo and cloth from Shu, brought by way of a country called Shendu: India.
Returns along the southern rim of the Tarim basin.
Captured by the Xiongnu again while trying to pass through Qiang territory.
Escapes in the confusion after the Shanyu's death and reaches Chang'an with one companion, Ganfu, after thirteen years.

name: Zheng He's second voyage
summary: Back out almost at once to take the envoys home and to invest the new king of Calicut, the fleet also calls at Siam and Cochin. At Calicut a stone is set up to record the Ming emperor's gifts.

stops.note: The fleet sails again within months.
Waiting for the monsoon.
A familiar first call.
Envoys to the king of Siam.
Ming envoys recognize Malacca's ruler.
The pepper kingdom south of Calicut.
A stone is set up to record the investiture of the new king.
Home in the summer.

name: Zheng He's third voyage
summary: On the third voyage the fleet fights its way out of Ceylon: the Sinhala king Alakeshvara is captured and taken to Nanjing. The trilingual stone at Galle, in Chinese, Tamil and Persian, dates from this voyage.

stops.note: The third fleet sets out.
Waiting for the monsoon.
A walled depot and warehouses are built at Malacca.
Northern Sumatra.
Leaves a stone in Chinese, Tamil and Persian giving offerings to the Buddha, to a Hindu god and to Allah.
Calicut and the pepper ports.
Ambushed on the way home, the fleet storms the capital and captures King Alakeshvara.
The captive king is brought before the emperor, then sent home.

name: Zheng He's fourth voyage
summary: The fleet goes beyond India for the first time, to Hormuz at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, the great market of the western Indian Ocean. Squadrons visit the Maldives and Bengal; the interpreter Ma Huan sails on this voyage and starts the notes that become his book.

stops.note: The fourth fleet sets out; Ma Huan sails as interpreter.
Waiting for the monsoon.
Through the depot at Malacca.
Ships are detached for Bengal.
Ceylon again.
Calicut, the turning point of earlier voyages.
The great market at the mouth of the Gulf: pearls, horses and every good of the West.
A squadron reaches Bengal, whose king sends a giraffe to the emperor.
Liushan, the 'Weak Water' islands.
Home with envoys from nineteen countries.

name: Zheng He's fifth voyage
summary: Taking home the envoys of nineteen countries, the fleet sails on to Aden and down the coast of East Africa, to Mogadishu, Brava and Malindi. It comes back with lions, leopards, ostriches, zebras and giraffes.

stops.note: The fifth fleet carries the foreign envoys home.
Waiting for the monsoon.
Through Calicut.
Hormuz again.
Adan: the king buys a giraffe and zebras to send to the emperor.
Mugudushu: houses of stone four or five storeys high, Fei Xin writes.
Malindi's envoys had brought a giraffe to Nanjing in 1415.
The fleet returns with envoys from seventeen countries and a menagerie.

name: Zheng He's sixth voyage
summary: Another fleet takes sixteen countries' envoys home. Squadrons under Zheng He's lieutenants reach the Arabian coast and East Africa again. Soon after, the Yongle emperor dies and his successor orders the voyages stopped.

stops.note: Envoys of sixteen countries are taken home.
Waiting for the monsoon.
Sumatra.
The squadrons part at Calicut.
Frankincense and dragon's blood.
Bulawa, on the Somali coast.
Home. The new emperor halts the voyages in 1424.

name: Zheng He's seventh voyage
traveler: Zheng He, Ma Huan and Fei Xin
summary: Called back by the Xuande emperor for one last voyage, the fleet sails to Hormuz; a squadron reaches East Africa, and seven men including Ma Huan travel from Calicut to Mecca. Zheng He dies on the way home. After this the fleets are never sent again, and the ships rot at their moorings.

stops.note: The last great fleet is assembled.
Zheng He sets up the Changle inscription recording all seven voyages.
Champa.
Malacca.
The fleet divides at Calicut.
The main fleet at Hormuz.
Seven men including the interpreter Ma Huan travel from Calicut to Mecca.
Zheng He dies, probably at sea off this coast.
The last fleet comes home. No fleet like it is sent again.

name: Zheng He's first voyage
summary: The Yongle emperor sends a fleet of some 62 great treasure ships and many smaller vessels, with about 27,000 men, into the Western Ocean. It calls at Champa, Java and Sumatra, reaches Calicut on the Malabar coast, and comes home with envoys and a captured pirate king.

stops.note: The first fleet, with about 27,000 men, is assembled.
The fleet waits for the north-east monsoon.
The first port of call.
Majapahit. Some 170 of the fleet's men are killed in a local war.
A sultanate at the northern tip of Sumatra.
A first call in Ceylon.
Guli, 'the great country of the Western Ocean': the voyage's goal.
On the way home, defeats the pirate chief Chen Zuyi and takes him to Nanjing.
Home with envoys from Calicut and other kingdoms.
